rule: Design progress bars to decelerate toward completion; users perceive faster completion when bars slow down at the end.
quote: An understanding of which behaviors perceptually shorten or lengthen process duration can be used to engineer a progress bar that appears faster

rule: Avoid linear progress bars; vary acceleration and deceleration to match human time perception rather than actual work completion.
quote: humans do not perceive the passage of time in a linear way. This, coupled with the irregular behavior of progress bars, produces a highly variable perception

rule: Distinguish retrieved facts from generated predictions in AI interfaces; users infer accuracy from fluency and mistake output style for truth.
quote: when the interface feels familiar and the writing sounds polished, it is easy to forget that the system is generating predictions rather than retrieving facts.

rule: Train users on AI capabilities and limitations before deployment; institutions roll out AI tools on productivity expectations while investing little in education.
quote: Organizations may roll out generative AI tools on the expectation that they will increase productivity, while investing little in education about limitations, bias, or verification.

rule: Provide individual feedback to each employee rather than team-wide praise to ensure they internalize it accurately.
quote: higher-ups may want to prioritize providing individual feedback to each employee to guarantee they will accurately relate the feedback back to themselves

rule: Display aggregate statistics and base rates alongside individual reviews or testimonials in product recommendations.
quote: we might ignore the product's two-star review on Amazon or the fact it had a sudden drop in sales quickly after its release

rule: Prioritize meeting agendas by importance and complexity; allocate time proportionally to task significance, not ease.
quote: you and your coworkers will likely find it much easier to talk about whether or not to get standing desks. As a result, everyone devotes a large portion of the scheduled meeting time to this more trivial matter

rule: Time promotions and special offers to coincide with payday and bonus periods when users have disposable income.
quote: marketers can time their advertising to coincide with when most people have disposable income or are receiving a bonus. This may mean on a Friday, when most people get their paycheck

rule: Avoid showing irrelevant numbers first; they become reference points that distort judgment of subsequent prices or values.
quote: The initial price of the earrings became your anchor point for evaluating subsequent pricing information, shifting your perspective on what constitutes a good deal.

rule: Present evidence and reasoning separately from the messenger's credentials; users struggle to detach message content from the status of who delivers it.
quote: The person's authority becomes the message itself. That is, we find it difficult to detach the content of the message from the status of the person delivering it.

rule: Require human review of automated recommendations before action; users trust automated tools more than their own judgment, even when contradictory evidence appears.
quote: You trusted the navigation system more than your own judgment, causing you to ignore what you saw with your own eyes.

rule: Show contradictory signals prominently when automated tools conflict with user observation; users often ignore gut feelings and external warnings that contradict automation.
quote: When we encounter contradictory information from another source or something feels off in our gut, we shouldn't ignore it.
finding: Prescribing errors increased 56.9% when clinical decision support gave incorrect recommendations vs. clinician judgment alone.

rule: Use opinion polls and majority signals cautiously; they cause moderate-minded users to abandon minority views and conform to the perceived majority.
quote: Opinion polls—regarding issues like climate change and gun control—caused ideologically moderate participants to abandon their minority opinions and conform to the majority, regardless of the topic.

rule: Place logo in top-left and search in top-right to match user expectations.
quote: Westerners tend to look at the top-left corner of a page first, so that's where the company logo should go. And most users also expect to see a search function in the top right.

rule: Provide citations and links to third-party sources to prove information accuracy.
quote: You can build web site credibility by providing third-party support (citations, references, source material) for information you present, especially if you link to this evidence.

rule: Show real people behind your organization; include employee bios with personal details.
quote: Show there are real people behind the site and in the organization. Next, find a way to convey their trustworthiness through images or text. For example, some sites post employee bios that tell about family or hobbies.

rule: Make contact information prominent: phone, address, and email.
quote: Make it easy to contact you. A simple way to boost your site's credibility is by making your contact information clear: phone number, physical address, and email address.

rule: Update content regularly and show recent review dates.
quote: Update your site's content often (at least show it's been reviewed recently). People assign more credibility to sites that show they have been recently updated or reviewed.

rule: Limit ads and distinguish sponsored content clearly; avoid pop-ups.
quote: Use restraint with any promotional content (e.g., ads, offers). If possible, avoid having ads on your site. If you must have ads, clearly distinguish the sponsored content from your own. Avoid pop-up ads, unless you don't mind annoying users and losing credibility.

rule: Fix typos, broken links, and downtime immediately; errors severely damage credibility.
quote: Avoid errors of all types, no matter how small they seem. Typographical errors and broken links hurt a site's credibility more than most people imagine. It's also important to keep your site up and running.

rule: Present information in digestible quantities; users cannot process all available data simultaneously due to cognitive limits.
quote: our limited ability to consider all the choices available to us, our incomplete knowledge of all the potential outcomes of our behavior

rule: Support satisficing decisions by highlighting the most relevant information; users optimize for good-enough choices, not perfect ones.
quote: bounded rationality encourages us to make decisions that satisfy a particular criterion, such as being ethical, without making the most optimal choice

rule: Show individual item prices clearly when offering bundles; bundling obscures per-item cost and reduces perceived waste.
quote: bundling leads to a decoupling of transaction costs and benefits. What this means is that bundling items together makes the cost of each individual item less obvious

rule: Show transaction friction for high-value purchases; digital payments reduce psychological pain and increase spending beyond intent.
quote: physically parting with cash triggers a psychological response—where we feel the pain of spending significantly more. The absence of physical notes and coins disrupts the mental connection

rule: Use friction to encourage intentional spending: require confirmation steps for digital transactions that users would reconsider with cash.
quote: Credit card payments and digital payments are also much faster, reducing the amount of time we have to reconsider a purchase that might be over our budget

rule: Limit product or option counts to reduce decision fatigue; more than 22 options significantly increases abandonment.
quote: One study found that offering shoppers more than 22 options increased the likelihood that they would not make any choice
finding: Offering >22 options increased likelihood of no purchase decision

rule: Highlight defaults early in multi-step decisions; users deplete decision-making capacity and revert to defaults later.
quote: people buying cars chose more default features at the end of the buying process than at the beginning, suggesting that selecting among various options earlier in the process had depleted their decision-making capacity
finding: Default feature selection increases after earlier choices deplete mental resources

rule: Present information that aligns with users' existing beliefs to reduce psychological discomfort and resistance.
quote: To create psychological consistency between his environmental beliefs and his not-so-environmental actions, John dismisses the lecture as misinformation

rule: Surface new information clearly when past commitments may no longer serve users' current goals.
quote: We continue engaging in behaviors that may have made sense in the past but are no longer rational, given the information we have now.

rule: Price options clearly and objectively so users compare based on actual value, not relative positioning.
quote: We tend to make decisions based less on which option best suits our purposes and more on what feels like the most advantageous choice.

rule: Signal automation failures visibly; operators overlook problems the system does not flag.
quote: decision makers miss problems the system does not flag and follow incorrect recommendations after good past performance

rule: Design AI aids to preserve operator judgment; framing as accurate erodes critical review under pressure.
quote: when tools are framed as accurate and efficient, people become more willing to lean on them and less inclined to question their recommendations, especially under time pressure

rule: Limit scope creep of automated systems; gradual expansion into new uses increases harm without governance upgrades.
quote: once in place, these systems are frequently expanded to new uses without a corresponding upgrade in governance or worker voice

rule: Separate option display to reduce overvaluing minor differences; joint comparison inflates perceived importance of trivial gaps.
quote: when we directly compare our options, we become hypersensitive to any differences that exist between them. This makes the differences seem glaringly obvious

rule: Invite feedback from peers and experts on your work; overconfident people resist learning and share unvetted information.
quote: overconfident individuals extremely resistant to being taught—since they believe they know the most—but they are also guilty of sharing the most information

rule: Prompt exploration of multiple solution paths; familiar approaches block discovery of more efficient alternatives.
quote: The Einstellung effect describes when we approach a problem with a mindset that worked for us in the past, even if a more efficient solution exists

rule: Avoid features that artificially increase perceived ownership; users will overvalue products they feel they own.
quote: any tactic that makes us feel a sense of psychological ownership over a product can encourage us to spend more on it

rule: Design free trials carefully: they create virtual ownership that leads users to pay for services they may not need.
quote: Free trials give us a sense of virtual ownership, or the feeling that we already own a product before we do, which can make us feel emotionally attached to a product before we decide to buy it

rule: Design reward schemes assuming users value intrinsic rewards; do not rely only on monetary incentives.
quote: you may incorporate some coupon codes to incentivize users. By neglecting the potential intrinsic rewards that may actually resonate more with a user than the extrinsic ones, you are failing to adequately optimize an incentive framework

rule: Design interfaces to suggest multiple affordances for common objects; avoid implying single purposes.
quote: Functional fixedness leads us to recognize only one affordance in an object when, in fact, there may be multiple

rule: Information learned in context is recalled more accurately than information accessed via search.
quote: information learned online is recalled less accurately than information learned from an encyclopedia

rule: Label products neutrally; health-related labeling inflates product ratings beyond actual quality.
quote: when the same food products are labeled either 'organic' or 'conventional,' the 'organic' products receive higher ratings and consumers are willing to pay more for them

rule: Show confidence calibration feedback; users overestimate ability on hard tasks and underestimate on easy ones.
quote: Our confidence usually doesn't match our actual ability, which can cause us to be ill-prepared when taking on hard tasks, and stress over easy tasks.

rule: Reserve heuristic shortcuts for low-stakes decisions; require careful reasoning for high-impact choices.
quote: The real problem occurs when we use heuristics for high-stakes decisions, where careful thought and objective rationality can help us avoid making serious errors.

rule: Show decision-makers the uncertainty they faced at the time; reveal prior alternatives to prevent overconfidence.
quote: Hindsight bias describes how we project this current knowledge onto the past, making it difficult to remember the uncertainty we initially faced

rule: Space repetitions of critical information over time rather than massing them together to improve long-term retention.
quote: the longer the time between repetitions of information, the more likely we are to commit that information to memory

rule: Link new information to existing knowledge or imagery rather than relying on structural repetition alone for deeper encoding.
quote: if we associate those terms with other information or imagery, it is encoded at a deep level and is easier to remember

rule: Encode information semantically by relating it to meaning, emotion, or prior knowledge rather than structurally or phonemically.
quote: A deep level of encoding occurs when we process information semantically, by associating it with emotion, idea or previous knowledge

rule: Highlight sunk costs as non-recoverable to help users make forward-looking decisions rather than past-protecting ones.
quote: the $100 is a sunk cost: it is spent, and no matter what you do, you will still be out $100

rule: Use credible messengers—trusted experts or authority figures—to present critical information or recommendations.
quote: If we believe the messenger is credible, then we are more likely to accept the information at face value

rule: Show users their full historical average alongside recent performance streaks to counter overconfidence in short-term trends.
quote: The hot hand fallacy leads us to take a small pool of data—the opening minutes of one game—as a better indicator of future performance than an average save percentage calculated from seasons' worth of data.

rule: In habit and progress trackers, warn users that recent success does not guarantee future performance and prepare them for inevitable plateaus and dips.
quote: Learning skills are never linear. There will always be ups and downs in our curve towards success. But the hot hand fallacy may cause us to only anticipate the upward trends when using these apps, rather than preparing us for the dips yet to come.

rule: Prompt explicit communication of intentions and feelings rather than relying on users to believe their state is obvious to others.
quote: Individuals might refrain from expressing their true feelings or concerns due to the illusion that others can easily discern their emotions.

rule: Recognize that confidence in predictions does not correlate with prediction accuracy; low information makes false certainty easier.
quote: The less information we have, the easier it is to put together a satisfying story, which can lead us to believe that we know more than we actually do.

rule: Do not assume causation from repeated coincidence; use caution when rare events cluster by time or place.
quote: We see that certain events consistently occur at the same time as, or just after, other events, leading us to conclude that they are somehow related.

rule: Beware that authority figures spreading false correlations increase public acceptance; verify sources before accepting novel claims.
quote: If the public learns about a flawed correlation between two events or factors from an individual with authority, they are more likely to accept it as truth.

rule: Limit repetition of statements; even one second exposure increases perceived truth, with largest effect after second encounter.
quote: all it takes is one repeated exposure of a given statement to increase our perception of truth
finding: largest effect occurs after second exposure

rule: Do not prioritize exciting features over usability; users adapt to environments slower than designers expect, so foundational reliability matters more.
quote: designers often prioritize a product's most exciting features while overlooking features that users actually want

rule: Use external incentives cautiously; over-reliance on rewards reduces intrinsic motivation and engagement once incentives are removed.
quote: relying on incentives can sap other intrinsic motivations to do things

rule: Present investment or resource-allocation options in a single unified list rather than separate category lists to reduce arbitrary equal distribution.
quote: When the investment options are listed together, we view them as all fitting into the same category. When they are listed separately, we view them as distinct categories.

rule: Use sequential rather than simultaneous choice presentation when decisions should reflect considered preference, not diversification bias.
quote: Simultaneous choice is when we are given multiple decisions to make at the same time, whereas sequential choice is when we make multiple decisions one after the other.
finding: 64% of simultaneous-choice participants selected three different options versus 9% of sequential-choice participants

rule: Test designs with users from multiple backgrounds, abilities, and cognitive styles to avoid assuming your perspective is universal.
quote: When designers assume their perspective is universal, they might conclude that their designs are inherently intuitive, overlooking usability challenges for people with different abilities, cognitive styles, or cultural backgrounds.

rule: Balance error messages and critical feedback with equal-weight positive reinforcement in error and state-change copy to counteract negativity bias.
quote: Negativity bias causes amplified emotional responses to negative events compared to positive events of equal magnitude.

rule: In marketing or persuasive copy, recognize that imagery evoking shared memories increases spending and social connectedness; use intentionally only for genuinely valuable offers.
quote: Nostalgia elicits feelings of social connectedness, making us feel as though we have a social network in which we belong.
finding: Participants writing nostalgic events felt more loved and protected than those writing non-nostalgic autobiographical events

rule: Minimize researcher-participant communication and environmental cues that hint at study hypotheses to prevent biased responses.
quote: demand characteristics are subtle cues from the experimenter that may give the participants some idea of what the study is about

rule: Surface concrete failure rates, base rates, and historical data prominently to counter optimism bias when users evaluate their own likelihood of success.
quote: Tom exhibits the optimism bias because he refuses to take into consideration the past six businesses that failed before him as well as the environmental factors working against him

rule: Show users the decision process and reasoning behind recommendations, not only the final outcome, to prevent outcome bias from distorting future trust.
quote: most postmortems are written as if the outcome was the only true measure of wisdom

rule: Present the most important information first in any sequence to maximize recall and decision influence.
quote: The primacy effect plays a crucial role in human memory, recall of items, learning, and even first impressions

rule: Place highest-rated or best-selling items at the top of lists to leverage positive first impressions on purchasing decisions.
quote: Marketers understand this and often highlight the most positive feedback first or structure websites so their best-selling or highest-rated items appear at the top

rule: In ballot, list, or choice interfaces, randomize order of equally valid options to prevent position bias from unfairly influencing selection.
quote: In 71 of the 79 elections, candidates who were listed first garnered more votes when listed first than when placed in other positions
finding: 71 of 79 elections showed primacy effect; in 7 cases the advantage exceeded the winner's victory margin

rule: Use semantically related words and concepts near each other to prime users toward desired associations and faster recognition.
quote: If you are first presented with the word 'doctor' a moment later, when presented with a list of unrelated words, you will recognize 'nurse' much faster than 'cat'

rule: Introduce achievement-related language in interface copy and messaging to increase user effectiveness and engagement.
quote: When a CEO primed his team with emails that contained achievement-related words (ex, prevail, accomplish, master), effectiveness rose by 15%, and efficiency rose by 35% over the workweek
finding: 15% increase in effectiveness, 35% increase in efficiency

rule: When presenting options, acknowledge that users' current emotional state may not reflect their future preferences and needs.
quote: We project our current state of hunger into our predictions of how much we could eat later and as a result waste money and food

rule: Repeat key steps or information throughout a sequential process, not just at the beginning, to prevent users forgetting critical steps.
quote: When presented with information in a sequential manner—that is, one after another—our brains are hardwired to remember the information that was most recently presented to us

rule: Avoid leading questions that subtly prompt respondents toward a particular answer.
quote: Leading questions can prompt survey-takers to respond in a certain way, even if it's not how they really feel. For example, in a customer-satisfaction survey a question like "Did you find our customer service satisfactory?" subtly leans towards a more favorable response, whereas asking the respondent to "Rate your customer service experience" is more neutral.

rule: Emphasize survey anonymity to reduce social desirability bias in sensitive questions.
quote: Emphasizing the anonymity of the survey can help reduce social desirability bias, as people feel more comfortable answering sensitive questions honestly when their names aren't attached to their answers.

rule: Design interfaces that acknowledge users' tendency to overestimate their self-control over impulses.
quote: When we underestimate the power of our impulses, we overestimate our own control over them.

rule: Highlight less visible but critical information to balance attention against emotionally striking details.
quote: While quickly detecting what is important and deserving of attentional resources is an important survival and learning mechanism, our predisposition to focus on the most prominent and emotionally striking details leads us to ignore potentially vital pieces of information.

rule: Account for users' tendency to recall positive aspects of past experiences more vividly when predicting future behavior.
quote: Overestimating the enjoyable moments of a previous event, or the positive results of past decisions, can impact what we decide to do in the future. We might be overconfident when making similar future decisions or overlook challenges we've experienced in the past.

rule: Design feedback mechanisms that encourage users to attribute failures to their own actions, not external factors.
quote: If we do not attribute our failures to our own errors, we are unlikely to learn from them in the future. Furthermore, refusing to acknowledge our mistakes makes us susceptible to repeating them down the line.

rule: Design conversational AI with warmth, name-use, and memory of user details to build trust and engagement.
quote: When an AI system speaks in a warm, conversational way, remembers details, and responds with empathy, people begin to feel a sense of relationship and safety.

rule: Avoid framing AI as a supportive partner or confidant unless intentionally managing disclosure risk and consent clarity.
quote: The more the relationship mimics that of a 'supportive partner,' behavioral recommendations may feel like relational obligations rather than optional suggestions.

rule: End user experiences with a positive moment or interaction to shape lasting memory of the entire experience.
quote: The peak-end rule influences our evaluations of experiences and can impact human behavior, decision making, and perceptions in both positive and negative ways.

rule: Highlight or create peaks during onboarding and key moments to anchor positive memory of the overall experience.
quote: We tend to recall an event based primarily on its most emotionally intense moments (both good and bad) and how it ends, rather than the entire experience as a whole.

rule: Display historical task duration or past project data to help users estimate timelines more realistically.
quote: A hallmark of the planning fallacy is that we tend to maintain our optimism about how long a task will take despite historical evidence that contradicts it.

rule: Highlight the most decisive differentiator when users choose between many similar options.
quote: The one that we choose is usually the first one that we determine adequately differentiates between options and makes our choice easy

rule: Use explicit dates or references when collecting time-based data; do not rely on user memory of when events occurred.
quote: it might be worthwhile to suggest referencing their email or credit card statement to increase the likelihood of getting accurate data

rule: Avoid strong-option UI for topics users understand poorly; users overestimate their knowledge and commit prematurely.
quote: people far too often hold strong opinions about topics for which they have limited information

rule: Place task-critical information at the beginning or end of lists; users remember first and last items best.
quote: presenting important information first or last on an interface guarantees users will store these items in their memory

rule: Limit visible items per screen to reduce cognitive load; let users filter to view fewer options at once.
quote: designers can allow users to activate filters so they only view a small number of clothing items instead of the entire stock

rule: Integrate guiding tools to help users encode small chunks of information progressively.
quote: Incorporating tools that guide users helps them encode small bits of information at a time

rule: Avoid bullet-point lists in AI responses; varied formatting reduces serial position effect reinforcement.
quote: language model AI often formats responses as bullet point lists to help enhance comprehensibility for users. However, this design feature may perpetuate the serial position effect even further

rule: Display source attribution prominently; avoid widgets that hide where facts come from.
quote: We don't encode the websites where we get our facts since we don't access the articles themselves. Instead, we merely browse through the search engine results page, which provides widgets containing exactly what we need to know

rule: Use neutral, unbiased language in prompts and questions; avoid leading language that plants false memories.
quote: if the officer had asked neutral questions—like 'How tall was the thief?' or 'What color was the thief wearing?'—Zachary would have been less likely to mistake her gender

rule: Distribute training or onboarding content over multiple sessions rather than in one session.
quote: By spacing out training sessions and incorporating well-placed follow-up content, organizations can improve employees' retention of important information

rule: Use injunctive norms (show what others approve) alongside descriptive norms for behavior change.
quote: Injunctive norms describe what people believe is approved or disapproved by others. That is, what society thinks you should do

rule: Communicate high expectations to users through interface design; expectations influence behavior and performance.
quote: others' expectations can greatly influence our performance. When someone thinks highly of us, we work hard to maintain that reputation.

rule: Avoid messaging that activates negative stereotypes; even subtle cues about group identity can harm task performance.
quote: Even subtle messaging that reminds people of the stereotypes about their social group can undermine people's performance.
finding: Female Asian Americans asked to report gender before a math test scored worse than those not; priming racial identity improved scores.

rule: When risk is emphasized in the interface, users overspend and purchase unnecessary services; balance risk information carefully.
quote: Zero risk bias is particularly strong in environments and situations where risk is emphasized, often leading to overspending and purchasing unnecessary services and items.

rule: Most users prefer eliminating small risks entirely over reducing larger risks; prioritize risk reduction, not elimination.
quote: if people are asked if they prefer the option to decrease a given risk from 5% to 0% or from 50% to 25%, most will opt for the former despite the drop from 50% to 25% being a far greater reduction in risk.
finding: Users choose zero risk over proportionally larger reductions in risk.

rule: Reduce options to speed decisions; more options leads to harder choices and slower decision-making.
quote: More options leads to harder decisions

rule: Make targets large and close to the cursor; large and close elements are easier to interact with.
quote: Large and close elements are easier to interact with

rule: Avoid banner placement for important messages; users learn to ignore repeatedly exposed elements.
quote: Users tune out the stuff they get repeatedly exposed to

rule: Frame information positively or negatively based on desired action; presentation format affects user decisions.
quote: The way information is presented affects how users make decisions

rule: Show social proof to influence behavior; users adapt actions based on what others do.
quote: Users adapt their behaviors based on what others do

rule: Tap into curiosity by revealing missing information gradually; users want to seek out gaps.
quote: Users have a desire to seek out missing information

rule: Match interface patterns to users' preconceived mental models; interfaces should align with how people think tasks work.
quote: Users have a preconceived opinion of how things work

rule: Prefer familiar experiences; users adapt more easily to designs they recognize.
quote: People prefer familiar experiences

rule: Use real-world object metaphors to ease adoption; users adapt more readily to skeuomorphic designs.
quote: Users adapt more easily to things that look like real-world objects

rule: Offer something first to trigger reciprocity; people feel compelled to give back when they receive.
quote: People feel the need to reciprocate when they receive something

rule: Highlight individual people, not groups, to increase engagement; users care disproportionately about individuals.
quote: Users care disproportionately about an individual as compared to a group

rule: Surprise with variable rewards; unexpected rewards engage users more than predictable ones.
quote: People especially enjoy unexpected rewards

rule: Create an aha moment early; users need to quickly realize your product's value.
quote: When new users first realize the value of your product

rule: Show progress toward goals to boost motivation; motivation increases as users approach completion.
quote: Motivation increases as users get closer to their goal

rule: Favor simple solutions; complexity should only exist when necessary.
quote: Simple solutions are often better than the more complex ones

rule: Highlight social responsibility features; users prefer socially responsible companies.
quote: Users tend to prefer socially responsible companies

rule: Show confidence ranges and multiple candidate answers to help users form accurate expectations and reduce overreliance on single outputs.
quote: Designers can show confidence ranges, highlight when a response is based on limited context, or present multiple candidate answers side by side.

rule: Place verify buttons beside copy buttons and ask confirmation before sending; prompt users to double-check medical, financial, or legal content.
quote: Small design choices such as placing a 'verify' button beside a 'copy' button, showing source links by default, or asking 'Does this look right?' before sending a message encourage reflection instead of automatic reuse.

rule: Track user corrections, overrides, and questions as healthy signals of engagement, not failures; avoid optimizing only for usage volume and satisfaction.
quote: Teams with higher AI literacy are more likely to track how often users correct, override, or question AI outputs and to treat those behaviors as healthy signals.

rule: Explain unfamiliar AI systems clearly to users; lack of clarity about how AI works increases hesitation to trust and adopt AI-assisted features.
quote: A lack of clarity prompts unease on the part of the patient, making them hesitant to follow through with the doctor's treatment plan.

rule: Ask users to generate counterarguments against initial anchor values during estimation or negotiation tasks to weaken anchoring effects.
quote: Half of the experts were also asked to come up with arguments against the anchor price. These participants showed a weaker anchoring effect compared to those who hadn't come up with counterarguments.
finding: experts who generated counterarguments showed weaker anchoring effect

rule: Assign a single, named decision owner accountable for each significant AI deployment's outcomes.
quote: For every significant AI deployment, assign a clearly identified "decision owner" who is accountable for outcomes in that domain.

rule: Map decision chains to expose where responsibility gaps exist in human-AI workflows.
quote: To counter accountability diffusion, teams can map decision chains. Besio and colleagues' work suggests that such mapping helps reveal where responsibility currently stops and where it needs to be strengthened.

rule: Design workflows where questioning AI output is expected and safe, not punished.
quote: Designing workflows where questioning the system is expected and safe.

rule: Enable iterative testing and genuinely solicit feedback to prevent developers from persisting with flawed product concepts.
quote: When developers or businesses cling to initial product concepts or marketing strategies without being receptive to feedback, they risk product failure.

rule: Request direct feedback or contributions from users rather than using intermediaries to maximize brand likeability.
quote: The results showed that the group who were asked to return their winnings directly by the researcher ended up liking him most. In other words, direct requests for a favor can increase likeability.
finding: direct favor requests increased likeability; indirect requests via intermediary decreased likeability

rule: Allow time between exposure to social signals and decision-making; delay decisions to reduce blind adoption of popular ideas.
quote: allowing some time to pass between noticing social signals and making our final decision can allow for critical thinking

rule: Foster psychological safety in teams by responding positively to dissent and experimentation; create space for minority opinions.
quote: creating psychological safety in the workplace can help break cycles of conformity among teams

rule: Recognize and avoid vague statements in copy that could apply to any user; make claims specific and verifiable.
quote: notice vague descriptions and generalized statements that could resonate with anyone

rule: Place the most important information at eye level; users choose visible options over equally good hidden alternatives.
quote: grocery stores can place the healthiest items at eye level to make us more likely to choose that option

rule: Avoid vague product labels or claims; users satisfice with misleading information rather than investigate further.
quote: Companies often label their products with enticing qualifiers with little-to-no meaning, such as the term 'cage-free' on a carton of eggs

rule: Time promotions to payday and bonus periods; satisfaction with purchases drops when spending depletes remaining budget.
quote: marketers can time their advertising to coincide with when most people have disposable income or are receiving a bonus
finding: Satisfaction dropped from 5.61 to 4.44 (1.17 point decrease on 1-9 scale) when purchase exhausted budget

rule: Offer special incentives at end-of-period; discounts and deals reduce pain of payment when budget depletes.
quote: marketers can also use these times as opportunities to use special incentives, like 2 for 1's or discounted rates

rule: Align payment timing with consumption; delay payment methods amplify dissatisfaction when bills arrive during budget shortfalls.
quote: when our bill comes, it is often at the end of the month which may coincide with the end of our budget

rule: Design interfaces to help users broaden focus when facing emotionally charged information by prompting consideration of multiple options.
quote: attentional bias shows up, however, we end up directing a much larger share of our focus toward a single option or stimulus, and this comes at the expense of others

rule: Use visual hierarchy to de-emphasize threat-related or emotionally negative content; anxious users fixate on threatening cues even when irrelevant.
quote: high-anxious individuals were slower to identify shapes, regardless of facial expression, suggesting that they were more fixated on facial cues, even if these cues were not necessarily threatening

rule: Present expert credentials and evidence as separate elements; users struggle to detach message content from messenger authority, leading to uncritical acceptance.
quote: we find it difficult to detach the content of the message from the status of the person delivering it

rule: Use symbols of authority (titles, badges, certificates) cautiously; subtle authority cues influence trust disproportionately to actual credibility.
quote: Subtle symbols of authority, such as a person's title (Dr, PhD, MD) or job title (CEO or Director), can immediately influence how we perceive the opinions and judgments of that individual

rule: Surface dissenting expert opinions and alternative perspectives with equal visual prominence to majority positions; users default to high-authority voices.
quote: Leaders or experts who are viewed as credible or high-status may have more influence on organizational decisions and strategies, potentially leading to important contributions from less authoritative employees being overlooked

rule: Require explicit human review and sign-off before automated systems execute high-stakes decisions; users trust automation more than their own judgment.
quote: Using a clinical decision support system increased prescribing errors by 56.9% when the system gave incorrect recommendations, compared to when clinicians relied on their own judgment without the tool
finding: 56.9% increase in prescribing errors when users relied on automated recommendations

rule: Limit automation to routine tasks only; apply human review to complex decisions involving multiple tradeoffs and uncertain outcomes.
quote: While automation did a great job of taking over routine tasks, when it was applied to more complex problems involving human decision-making, people were more likely to make mistakes

rule: Define which decisions AI may make alone, which require human review with criteria, and which must remain human-led.
quote: Organizations can map tasks into tiers: low-stakes routine, medium-stakes judgment, and high-stakes critical decisions. For each tier, they can specify which tasks AI may perform alone, which require human review with clear criteria, and which must remain human-led.

rule: Provide clear appeal processes and explanation mechanisms so affected people can contest AI-influenced decisions.
quote: Clear appeal processes, explanation mechanisms, and support for contesting outcomes can help surface harms and boundary breaches early.

rule: Physically separate bundled items at purchase and display, even if monetarily bundled, to make per-item costs visible.
quote: physically separating the items can ensure consumers actually get the full value of their purchase
finding: Participants shown bundled pass rated likelihood of use 3.9/10; monetarily bundled but physically unbundled 5.4/10; both unbundled 6.74/10

rule: Require users to consciously calculate per-item cost before confirming bundle purchases to counteract bundling bias.
quote: calculate the cost of each individual item, to see how much of the package we would have to use to make our purchase worth it

rule: Add confirmation steps and friction for digital transactions to restore the psychological pain of payment and reduce impulsive overspending.
quote: Credit card payments and digital payments are also much faster, reducing the amount of time we have to reconsider a purchase

rule: Limit choice sets to 22 or fewer options to maintain purchase intent and reduce decision paralysis.
quote: offering shoppers more than 22 options increased the likelihood that they would not make any choice
finding: More than 22 options: 3% jam booth purchase rate vs. 30% with 6 options; shoppers abandonment increases significantly

rule: Separate browsing intent from purchase intent; allow users to explore options without commitment pressure to reduce cognitive load.
quote: we are less likely to feel the effects of choice overload when we don't put any pressure on ourselves to commit to one option
finding: Separation of exploration from decision-making reduces cognitive exhaustion and improves satisfaction

rule: Frame choices as final or nonreversible to reduce post-choice regret and rumination, even if returns are technically possible.
quote: treating your choices as nonreversible (even if they technically are) can shut down this process before it gets started
finding: Perceived finality reduces regret and post-decision rumination

rule: Provide expert or domain-specific information to users with low knowledge to prevent paralysis when faced with many options.
quote: when consumers are considered to be experts in a domain, the effect of choice overload is reversed
finding: 401(k) enrollment: 65% low-knowledge with many funds vs. 88% with high knowledge; 80% low-knowledge with few funds vs. 65% high-knowledge

rule: Design for exploratory thought by prompting users to consider multiple viewpoints before deciding, not just rationalizing one belief.
quote: exploratory thought, which takes into consideration many viewpoints before deciding where you stand

rule: Encourage debate and interpersonal discussion in decision workflows to expose users to information they may have otherwise avoided.
quote: Engaging in debate is a productive way to challenge our views and expose ourselves to information we may have otherwise avoided

rule: Schedule critical decisions and important meetings early in the day, before cognitive resources deplete.
quote: we also make better decisions earlier in the day. To avoid decision fatigue, we can schedule work meetings and critical decision-making at the beginning of the day

rule: Reduce the number of choices users must make per task; deploy AI or defaults to eliminate low-value decisions.
quote: Reducing necessary choices or decisions is a common technique used to curb decision fatigue

rule: Limit visible product or option counts to prevent choice overload; 74% of shoppers abandon carts when overwhelmed by options.
quote: 74% of shoppers say they have abandoned their online shopping cart because they were too overwhelmed by all the options
finding: 74% abandonment rate due to option overload

rule: Use decision-minimization tools to guide users through large option sets; tested approach reduced decisions by 39% while increasing satisfaction.
quote: it decreased the number of decisions by 39% compared to heuristic strategies and by 20% relative to standard recommendation systems. Users were also found to be more satisfied
finding: 39% reduction in decisions; improved satisfaction vs heuristics

rule: Ensure users eat or maintain blood glucose before decision-heavy workflows; glucose replenishment reverses ego depletion and improves choice quality.
quote: supplying glucose helped individuals mitigate ego depletion and sometimes completely reversed it. The replenished willpower would enhance people's capacity for self-control and improve their decision-making abilities
finding: Glucose supply reverses ego depletion

rule: Show investors their long-term portfolio performance, not individual stock gains or losses, to reduce emotional trading.
quote: providing investors with a graph that showed their total portfolio performance helped shift their focus from individual stock gains/losses to overall wealth accumulation
finding: Goal-setting plus performance visualization reduced or reversed the disposition effect; investors with clear targets exhibited reversed disposition effect

rule: Use 360-degree feedback systems so employees see their performance rated by multiple sources, not just their own self-assessment.
quote: Implement 360-degree feedback systems to give employees a well-rounded view of their performance, helping them better understand their strengths and areas for improvement

rule: Display objective performance metrics alongside self-ratings to align employee self-perception with measurable reality.
quote: Use Objective Metrics: Rely on data-driven performance metrics to provide employees with a clear, accurate picture of their progress

rule: In team or collaborative tools, explicitly surface dissent and minority opinions to counter groupthink.
quote: Groupthink occurs when groups strive to reach a consensus while minimizing conflicts, causing individuals to set aside their opinions in favor of the group majority

rule: Seek real-world data and diverse user feedback rather than projecting your own preferences onto product design decisions.
quote: Instead of assuming that others share your views or preferences, seek hard data to confirm or refute these assumptions

rule: When presenting pricing tiers, frame the middle option as the best value to discourage selection of the cheapest plan.
quote: the middle tier is often framed as the best value option, discouraging users from opting for the cheapest plan

rule: Frame new technology features as enhancing human ability and saving time, not as replacing human skills or invading privacy.
quote: emphasizing how AI can enhance our human abilities, help us save time, or reduce our workloads rather than pointing out its potential to take our jobs

rule: Design for users in distress by incorporating lived-experience feedback, not assumptions from calm states.
quote: A designer who hasn't got technical support from a professional psychologist may struggle to anticipate the needs, emotions, and decision-making processes of users who are experiencing distress, anxiety, or depression

rule: Present objects with multiple visual contexts or uses to help users recognize diverse affordances beyond conventional functions.
quote: seeing pictures led participants to rely more on existing, top-down knowledge when generating unusual uses, resulting in less innovative responses than when they were exposed only to object names
finding: Pictures reduced creative problem-solving compared to verbal descriptions alone

rule: Provide clear prompt guidance and examples to help users supply sufficient context, preventing them from blaming AI tools for poor outputs due to vague inputs.
quote: Most will stress the importance of being detailed and specific, as well as providing clear context to the problem you wish to solve

rule: Avoid designing interfaces that reward streak-based confidence; surface base rates and historical failure rates to counter false control beliefs.
quote: a short streak of early wins—often called 'beginner's luck'—can dramatically inflate a person's perceived control over random outcomes

rule: In uncertain systems, show users the limits of their influence and provide structured, systematic decision tools instead of relying on intuition.
quote: those in charge often overestimated their ability to predict and manage the future through individual foresight practices, rather than relying on formal, systematic foresight methods

rule: Surface base rates and objective statistics alongside individuating details in prediction or recommendation contexts; do not rely on pattern consistency alone.
quote: we tend to ignore base rate information in favor of individuating information

rule: Require critical analysis of missing information and alternative outcomes before committing to high-stakes decisions; prompt contingency planning.
quote: Coming up with alternate predictions or developing contingency plans can help you prepare for different outcomes than the one you predicted

rule: Present factual claims in statement form, not opinion form, to reduce illusory truth effects.
quote: information presented as fact (e.g., "The diameter of the moon is 2,160 miles") is more likely to produce the illusory truth effect than information presented as opinion

rule: Evaluate truthfulness of claims on first encounter; users who assess accuracy avoid illusory truth effects better than those who evaluate interestingness.
quote: when participants had initially been asked to evaluate truthfulness instead of interestingness, they didn't show signs of the illusory truth effect

rule: Warn users that familiar statements feel true even when false; awareness of processing fluency helps resist illusory truth.
quote: ease of processing is our go-to tool to judge whether something is true, and it's only if that fails that we turn to our knowledge for help

rule: Help users broaden focus when predicting outcomes; narrowly focused predictions inflate expected emotional impact by 20–40 percent.
quote: thinking about other future events or activities, rather than fixating on one, helps us acknowledge their collective influence on our future emotions. Studies show that people moderate their emotional forecasts when they think more broadly about their upcoming experiences

rule: Prime users toward long-term thinking via words like 'future' and 'long-term' to reduce impulsive choices.
quote: being exposed to words like 'future,' 'long-term,' and 'self-control' actually made participants more likely to think of themselves and their future

rule: Use specific named individuals with photos, not statistics, to drive donations and engagement.
quote: statistics feel impersonal and cold whereas we can often visualize a particular individual in need
finding: Donations for single named child 11.4 SEK (~$1.31 USD) higher than for two identifiable children

rule: Show specific impact and outcomes tied to individual stories, not aggregate statistics.
quote: charities can market their cause in a manner that is more likely to get them donations and help. Instead of relying on statistics, they may distribute materials that showcase a particular individual

rule: Explicitly invite users to feel emotion; suppress default emotional regulation to increase help for multiple victims.
quote: when prompted to allow ourselves to feel emotions, the identifiable victim effect can be reduced
finding: Participants allowing emotions showed no difference in compassion between single and eight-victim scenarios; those suppressing emotions showed large difference

rule: Ensure assembly or creation tasks are simple enough to succeed; failed completion destroys the effect.
quote: when people failed to complete the box-building project or destroyed their Lego creations, the effect dissipated

rule: Ask users for external feedback on self-made work to counteract overconfidence bias.
quote: A simple strategy to deal with this is to make a habit of asking others for feedback

rule: Encourage handwritten note-taking over passive reading to strengthen memory encoding.
quote: Taking hand-written notes instead of just skimming also helps us actively store facts in our long-term memory

rule: Provide frequent retrieval opportunities for learned material; memory strength depends on retrieval frequency.
quote: the strength of memory is directly tied to how frequently memories are retrieved
finding: Memory strength correlates with retrieval frequency

rule: Show information location explicitly when saving or storing; users remember access paths better than content.
quote: participants better recalled which statements were saved than which were erased, suggesting that when we believe we will be able to access the information later, we remember how to access it rather than the information itself
finding: Users recall access paths better than content when believing information is saved

rule: Use neutral product labels; health-related or premium labeling inflates perceived quality beyond actual product performance.
quote: when the same food products are labeled either 'organic' or 'conventional,' the 'organic' products receive higher ratings and consumers are willing to pay more
finding: Organic labeling increases perceived quality and willingness to pay versus identical conventional-labeled products

rule: Reserve System 1 thinking for low-stakes decisions; switch to System 2 deliberation for choices with significant consequences.
quote: the goal is to use heuristics for decisions that don't require effortful, conscious thought—like deciding what to eat for breakfast—while switching to careful reasoning for high-stakes decisions, such as managing our finances or hiring employees.

rule: In complex information contexts, actively seek diverse sources rather than relying on easily accessible or memorable examples.
quote: heuristics can be avoided by making judgments more effortfully, but in doing so, we must actively seek diverse information and evidence instead of relying solely on information that is easily accessible and available.

rule: Ask users to log decisions and their predictions before outcomes are known to create an unalterable record and prevent memory distortion.
quote: keep track of your past decisions and their associated predictions. This can be done in what's known as a 'decision journal'

rule: Base AI system predictions on large historical datasets, not recent successful outputs, to prevent over-reliance when the algorithm shows a streak of quality.
quote: when algorithms chug out numerous high-quality outputs in a row, we may expect the same level of quality for all future outputs. Statistically speaking, perfection is impossible

rule: Avoid rewarding high-effort tasks with external incentives; incentives reduce creativity and risk-taking by pushing users toward the easiest solution rather than the best one.
quote: When people have been offered a reward to do something, they try to make the job as easy as possible, minimizing difficulty. This results in less creativity

rule: When marketing fair-trade or ethical products, emphasize concrete consumer agency and impact rather than highlighting injustice alone; frame choices as direct remedies, not distant moral obligations.
quote: if they are shown that their purchases can actively help reduce injustice, they become more likely to buy fair-trade products
finding: Consumers perceiving high injustice with no clear fix were less likely to support fair trade; showing direct causal impact of purchases increased likelihood.

rule: Design decision-support interfaces to prompt System 2 thinking (deliberate, slower analysis) by forcing users to review full context and alternative explanations before finalizing judgments about people or outcomes.
quote: Slowing down the process by which we make our judgments and considering all of the information at hand allows us to make better decisions

rule: For retention beyond 7 days, space review sessions at least one day apart; for longer delays, extend spacing to 10 days or more.
quote: the optimal length of time for teachers to repeat information to students is likely between one and ten days
finding: At 7-day test: 1-day lag optimal; at 35-day test: both 1-day and 10-day lags outperformed same-day review

rule: Provide reference points and distribution information for attributes difficult to evaluate in isolation (e.g., horsepower, GPA, experience count).
quote: when it's difficult to evaluate an object in isolation, people tend to think about other objects in the same category to use as a reference point
finding: Without programming experience context, people favored lower-experience candidate with high GPA; with both candidates shown together, they favored higher-experience candidate

rule: Minimize salience of negative attributes on superior options; ensure positive attributes are equally prominent across all choices.
quote: people's impressions of the objectively superior option are often handicapped by a highly salient, negative feature

rule: Link new interface information to users' existing knowledge, emotions, or passions rather than relying on repetition alone.
quote: if we associate new information with something meaningful, we are more likely to remember it

rule: Design interfaces assuming users have different mental models; test with diverse users to uncover perspective gaps.
quote: Designers might not realize how much of their perspective is shaped by their experience and knowledge—and that most users don't possess the same understanding that they do.

rule: Actively seek negative usability feedback; treat it as design truth, not user error.
quote: designers might attribute negative responses to user error, missing key opportunities to improve the product for their intended users

rule: Respond visibly to negative reviews in product interfaces; inaction amplifies negative perception.
quote: Managing and responding to negative reviews in a constructive and public manner can help to mitigate these effects.

rule: Do not rely on halo effects from social responsibility to mask product quality gaps.
quote: we are more likely to use the halo effect to form judgments regarding the quality of products sold at a store when we are unfamiliar with that type of product

rule: Frame options highlighting potential gains rather than risks to reduce loss-averse decision-making.
quote: Phrasing a question as a loss may increase loss aversion, while phrasing that same question as a gain may reduce loss aversion, leading to a more calculated response.

rule: Understand that loss intensity is roughly twice as powerful as equivalent gain in user motivation and decision-making.
quote: losses are twice as powerful compared to their equivalent gains, a foundational concept of prospect theory.
finding: 2x multiplier: loss impact versus equivalent gain

rule: Segregate gains visually and in messaging; integrate losses to reduce perceived pain of larger purchases.
quote: people are generally happiest when gains are segregated and losses are integrated. Even if the outcome is the same, we respond very differently depending on how things are presented.

rule: Show sunk costs as already spent and non-recoverable; emphasize forward-looking value to prevent sunk-cost-fallacy decisions.
quote: the $100 is a sunk cost: it is spent, and no matter what you do, you will still be out $100. If the costs of getting to the concert venue are greater than the pleasure you will get from seeing the show, then at the end of the day, going will result in a worse outcome than staying home.

rule: Use premortem exercises to help teams imagine failure modes before launch; ask what could go wrong and why.
quote: Make a premortem: humans are really good at revisiting and dissecting past negative events to try to understand the cause. While postmortems look backwards, premortems imagine potential disasters and explore their likely causes.

rule: Make multiple forecasts (low, medium, high estimate) for outcomes instead of planning for a single scenario.
quote: Make three estimates or forecasts for the future: when predicting a potential outcome, make a low, medium, and high estimate.

rule: Recognize that nostalgic design increases perceived social connectedness, making money feel less important; this effect is specific to spending, not time.
quote: participants who had recalled a nostalgic memory gave away more money, but not more time, than participants who had recalled a neutral memory

rule: Use double-blind study design where neither participants nor researchers know group assignment to prevent unconscious bias in treatment.
quote: A double-blind research design can be effective in preventing the observer expectancy effect. In studies with this design, neither the participants nor the researchers know which participants are in the experimental group or which are in the control group.

rule: Avoid leading questions and treat all study groups identically; even subtle verbal or non-verbal cues from researchers influence participant behavior.
quote: researchers may ask participants leading questions, which prompt a specific response, or even treat participants in a way that elicits the desired behavior

rule: When presenting opposing viewpoints or critical information, attribute them to highly credible sources to increase acceptance likelihood by 3x.
quote: When readers were told that a credible author wrote the opposing viewpoint, they were three times more likely to change their opinion than those who thought the source was not credible.
finding: Credible source attribution increased opinion change by 300%.

rule: Use pediatrician-created or endorsed health materials rather than generic content to increase parent adoption of self-care resources for minor childhood illnesses.
quote: parents were more likely to use self-diagnosis charts and home treatment resources if pediatricians approved or created the material.

rule: Frame promotions as gamified chances to win rather than guaranteed discounts to increase engagement and resource investment.
quote: a more effective means of garnering customer interest would be to hold a promotion such as 'win a chance at a free sweater when you spend 200.00$ or more!' The uncertain reward generates more excitement

rule: Use variable reward schedules in reward programs rather than fixed rewards to sustain user engagement and reduce task abandonment.
quote: Variable schedules are more unpredictable, which makes the behavior less prone to extinction. Behavioral extinction is when an organism ceases to engage in a certain learned behavior and it happens less quickly for randomized, rather than fixed schedules.

rule: Default to user benefit in bundled features; avoid pre-checked boxes that exploit omission bias to charge for unwanted extras.
quote: When additional features are bundled with a product or service by default, such as checked luggage and seat selection on a plane fare, omission bias may make users less likely to opt-out

rule: Store payment methods by default to reduce checkout friction and lower cart abandonment via omission bias.
quote: shopping apps commonly have a default option to store credit card information for future purchases, making it less likely that a customer will abandon their shopping cart

rule: Surface base rates and historical failure data to ground user estimates in reality and counter optimism bias.
quote: Look for statistics on how long it takes to complete the type of task on average. These are your base rates

rule: Use premortem exercises: ask teams to imagine project failure and list causes before launch to surface blind spots.
quote: Everyone on the team is instructed to imagine it is a year from the present and the project has failed. They are then instructed to write out what has gone wrong and why.

rule: Break goals into specific, measurable milestones and display progress visibly to motivate monitoring and counter avoidance.
quote: set clear, specific goals and break them into manageable steps so you can track your progress with objective measures

rule: Record decision reasoning, assumptions, and uncertainties before outcomes occur; compare afterward against actual information available.
quote: Encourage decision-makers to record their reasoning before key choices: assumptions, data sources, alternative options, and known uncertainties.

rule: Separate learning reviews (system behavior, weak signals) from accountability reviews; hold both conversations.
quote: A learning review that focuses on system behavior, weak signals, tradeoffs, and how similar events can be prevented. A formal accountability review that applies clear standards to individual conduct.

rule: Use positive feedback and verbal praise over tangible or monetary rewards; verbal reinforcement maintains intrinsic motivation longer.
quote: Participants who received these verbal rewards maintained their motivation across puzzle-solving sessions—even after removing them—while control groups showed declining motivation.
finding: Verbal rewards preserved intrinsic motivation; tangible rewards reduced it over time.

rule: Place transparent non-human disclosures at moments of high compliance (onboarding, first use, sensitive flows) with plain language.
quote: Use clear, repeated disclosures in onboarding, first use, and sensitive flows, with plain language such as 'I am an AI system that predicts text based on patterns in data.'

rule: Separate relational warmth (emotional processing) from high-stakes guidance (money, medicine, law) with distinct decision paths and human review.
quote: Let the chatbot provide warmth for emotional processing, then route decisions about medication, money, or legal steps into a separate 'decision support' path with tighter framing, extra prompts, and human review.

rule: Add deliberate friction before major decisions: offer step-back prompts showing alternatives people in similar situations consider.
quote: Use step-back prompts before major decisions, such as 'Here are the alternatives people in your situation often consider.'

rule: Let users control relational tone: offer settings to dial warmth up or down, choose context memory, and select proactive topics.
quote: Systems can offer settings that let people dial the tone up or down, choose when the AI remembers context, and control what kinds of topics it can proactively raise.

rule: End product interactions on a high note, ensuring the final moment leaves a strong positive emotional impression.
quote: by ending experiences on a high note, it's typical that they will be remembered in a more positive light

rule: Create measurable peaks during critical moments in user flows to anchor positive recall of the entire experience.
quote: we tend to recall an event based primarily on its most emotionally intense moments (both good and bad) and how it ends

rule: End conversational AI interactions with warm, personalized closing statements to create positive memory of the entire exchange.
quote: polite the bot is when your conversation comes to an end. It may leave you with a personalized, warm response such as "I'm glad I could help!

rule: Break large projects into smaller subtasks for estimation; users estimate small task completion accurately but consistently underestimate large ones.
quote: we are much better at planning for small ones: often, our estimates are remarkably accurate, and at worst, they are overestimates
finding: Users estimate completion time accurately for small tasks but significantly underestimate large projects.

rule: Display historical completion data from similar past tasks to help users set realistic timelines for new projects.
quote: If an organization or individual has completed similar projects in the past, they can use the outcomes of those previous experiences to set goals for new ones

rule: Prompt round-table discussion where each member shares views individually to break assumed agreement and surface actual disagreement.
quote: prompting a round-table discussion where each member shares their opinion can break the cycle of assumed agreement

rule: Place most critical content and highest-rated items at the start of sequences to maximize recall and positive framing.
quote: students are more likely to remember information introduced at the beginning of a learning session, it makes sense to front-load the most critical content early

rule: Vary sequence and repeat key points throughout content to reduce overreliance on first-presented information.
quote: Try to vary the sequence or repeat key points throughout to reduce overreliance on what comes first

rule: Preview study materials before high-stakes tasks to reduce error rates and improve learning outcomes.
quote: letting students preview a study list for an upcoming exam—can help reduce error rates and improve learning outcomes

rule: Avoid applying time-limited discounts or offers at moments of peak emotional engagement; defer decision points to a neutral emotional state.
quote: A ski resort offering you a 10% discount on an annual pass when people return their equipment at the end of using a day pass. They are banking on the projection bias; that, in the moment, we will overestimate how many times we will come skiing that year

rule: In negotiation flows, present concession lists tied to prior user-stated preferences to reduce devaluation of offers.
quote: the concessions she makes will be explicitly linked to the preferences he has stated. Consequently, when Jack receives this proposal there is less of a chance that he will say, 'Well.. if Jill is offering this up to me it must not have any value' and reject it

rule: Offer users a menu of concession choices rather than a single proposal to maintain their sense of control and reduce rejection of fair offers.
quote: creating 'concession menus', where we create a list of choices of concessions that the other party can pick from. This initiates a back-and-forth between the two parties and allows each side to maintain some level of control

rule: Offer middle-ground response options to prevent acquiescence bias in survey scales.
quote: acquiescence bias, which is the tendency to agree with all "Yes/No" or "Agree/Disagree" questions

rule: Keep surveys brief to prevent extreme responding when respondents disengage from longer questionnaires.
quote: it's important to factor in length when designing a survey or structured interview. If it's too long, participants may zone out and respond less carefully

rule: Smokers who believed they had high impulse control chose higher temptation levels and were significantly more likely to smoke.
quote: smokers who received results for high-control of their impulses were more likely to choose a higher level of temptation than the low-control group
finding: high-control belief group had significantly higher smoking rate

rule: Display source attribution directly on search results and information widgets; do not hide citations behind clicks.
quote: We don't encode the websites where we get our facts since we don't access the articles themselves. Instead, we merely browse through the search engine results page, which provides widgets containing exactly what we need to know.

rule: Citation systems in AI must display sources or acknowledge when sources are absent; do not provide detailed answers without indicating source provenance.
quote: ChatGPT provides a lengthy response that distinguishes official languages from regional and even extinct ones. However, while Google directly links its answer to its source, ChatGPT does not cite a single one

rule: Avoid leading questions in legal or high-stakes contexts; resist phrasing that suggests an answer or detail (e.g., "the gun" vs. "any weapon").
quote: Did you see the gun, or did the officer tell you there was a gun? Did the cars smash into each other, or did the attorney simply suggest they did?

rule: Slow the presentation pace of sequential information and avoid verbal-only delivery to reduce recency effect strength.
quote: the recency effect is stronger for longer lists of items and tends to occur more when the information is presented verbally rather than visually

rule: Users recall the final 2–3 items in a sequence with double the accuracy of middle items; design accordingly.
quote: the probability of recalling the first and last items on a list could be up to two times that of items in the middle of the list
finding: Probability of recall for first and last items can be up to 2x that of middle items

rule: Downward anticipated regret (fear of missing out) drives impulse buying more than upward regret (price drop); emphasize FOMO cautiously.
quote: shoppers who experienced downward anticipated regret were more likely to engage in online impulsive buying. In contrast, the participants who experienced upward anticipated regret demonstrated less impulsive behavior
finding: Downward regret (not buying) triggers more impulse buying than upward regret (price drop)

rule: Larger sample sizes override intuitive category matching; emphasize n-size when users judge probability from samples.
quote: James drew a greater sample of balls than Sally, so he is in a better position to judge the contents of the jar

rule: Display real-time feedback about consequences of user actions to counteract focus on vivid, immediate factors.
quote: Studies have shown real-time feedback on a specific behavior can induce significant behavioral changes. When individuals are made aware of the consequences of their behavior as it occurs, they are more likely to adapt and make smarter choices.
finding: Consumers who saw daily energy use from showering significantly reduced consumption patterns; restaurants displaying caloric information reduced caloric intake.

rule: Use bullet points and visual highlighting in AI-generated responses to make important information stand out.
quote: Large language machines such as ChatGPT use the salience bias to present important information in a way that will stand out more to the user. Responses are often presented in bullet point form with salient information highlighted for ease of retrieval.

rule: Avoid defensive error messaging; frame product failures as opportunities for user improvement, not blame.
quote: In the event that a customer is displeased with a product, a primary instinct may be to defend the project or pin the blame on the user for incorrect use. However, this can translate to further customer dissatisfaction and a missed opportunity for redemption.

rule: Vary the order of list items across multiple exposures so each item occupies different serial positions.
quote: Instead of repeatedly studying the five facts in the same order, you might want to write them down in a different order the second time you go through them. That means that different items will be at the beginning, middle, and end of the series.
finding: Rearranging item order increases recall of middle items.

rule: Avoid using bullet-point lists in AI responses; use varied formatting to reduce primacy and recency dominance.
quote: The order in which machine learning generates outputs affects what pieces of information we encode and store in our memory. This is especially true since language model AI often formats responses as bullet point lists to help enhance comprehensibility for users. However, this design feature may perpetuate the serial position effect even further.

rule: Limit single learning sessions to 30 minutes with breaks between to maintain retention.
quote: A typical recommendation for learning sessions is 30 minutes long, with breaks to split up these sessions.

rule: Use AI to predict and deliver content at each user's optimal review intervals based on their retention patterns.
quote: AI systems to 'predict' the best time for each learner to review information, enhancing long-term retention and engagement

rule: Assume users underestimate how little others notice their actions, appearance, or mistakes in interfaces.
quote: people are less likely to notice our mistakes and shortcomings than we expect

rule: Change default options to guide users toward optimal choices, not merely accept the existing norm.
quote: the first group tended to choose the option framed as the default—even when the second group did not choose that option any more than the others

rule: Reduce choice overload by limiting visible options to avoid users defaulting to status quo from decision paralysis.
quote: the strength of the status quo bias is positively correlated with the number of options in a choice set

rule: Automate beneficial changes to defaults so users benefit from optimal choices without active effort.
quote: investors are rewarded by doing nothing, as the default option automatically shifts funds towards the optimal assets for their age group

rule: Present information in neutral, organized language; disorganized or unclear subject matter increases suggestibility.
quote: lack of knowledge or flawed organization surrounding the subject matter being conveyed can also impact a person's level of suggestibility

rule: Disclose full study parameters: sample size, dropout rates, and duration when presenting trial or product results.
quote: What was the sample size? Did people drop out of the study? How long did they use the product for? All of these questions are important

rule: Offer 2–3 top criteria instead of all criteria when helping users compare alternatives; middle ground beats both extremes.
quote: It might be best when making choices between alternatives, to use a decision-making process that falls somewhere in the middle. You might identify the top two or three criteria

rule: In surveys asking users to recall past events, provide reference aids like email or credit card statements to ground estimates in concrete data rather than memory.
quote: it might be worthwhile to suggest referencing their email or credit card statement to increase the likelihood of getting accurate data from the respondent

rule: Require users to explain their understanding or reasoning before committing to high-consequence decisions; forced explanation reveals knowledge gaps and reduces overconfidence.
quote: having to explain your knowledge brings you to realize how limited it is in reality
finding: When researchers asked participants to explain a political policy in detail before seeing counter-arguments, they rated their understanding lower but were actually less likely to change their position, suggesting explanation reduces overconfidence and increases commitment to accurate views.

rule: Break complex explanations into discrete, levelized steps; users confuse the ability to describe components or levels with true understanding of how systems work together.
quote: being able to describe different levels of an item or concept inflates our perception of how much we know about it

rule: Communicate high expectations to users through tone, design, and feedback; expectations influence task effort and actual performance outcomes.
quote: others' expectations can greatly influence our performance. When someone thinks highly of us, we work hard to maintain that reputation
finding: Teachers' expectations of students predicted math achievement even three semesters later; high expectations increased students' own academic self-concept, which predicted future performance.

rule: Offer free cancellation and no-contract options to eliminate switching costs and increase adoption.
quote: no-contract plans and free cancellation policies for mobile phone services and internet packages can help eliminate the risk of being locked into a long-term commitment. If a customer knows they can opt out whenever they want without a penalty, they are more likely to sign up.

rule: Hold AI tools to realistic error rates; users accept 11.3% error from humans but only 6.8% from AI, creating unfair standards.
quote: people have significantly lower acceptable error rates for AI (6.8%) than humans (11.3%).
finding: AI acceptable error rate: 6.8%; human acceptable error rate: 11.3%

rule: Expose complex features progressively to reduce cognitive overwhelm during onboarding.
quote: Users are less overwhelmed if they're exposed to complex features later
